text: Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines were built for high-throughput ETL tolerating latencies from seconds to minutes — never for in-the-loop decisions needing tens of milliseconds, like fraud scoring or live personalization. Until now, meeting that bar meant bolting on a second specialized engine like Apache Flink. Real-Time Mode removes that second engine, targeting p99 latency in the tens to low hundreds of milliseconds, inside the exact same declarative authoring model.

Two primitives do the work, and notice what's absent: no writeStream, no awaitTermination, no checkpoint paths to manage by hand. You declare an external sink — often Lakebase — and define an update flow that targets it. The switch is one line: pipelines.trigger set to RealTime. And pipelines.trigger.interval isn't a batch size — it only governs how often state and offsets get checkpointed.

Databricks' own demo tracks live aircraft positions from Kafka. The stateful flow answers a question no single record can answer alone: how many aircraft are in each monitored zone right now? It's built as one keyed stateful operator — one shuffle, one hop — holding a map of aircraft to last-seen time, using the Arbitrary Stateful Processing API.

Two patterns worth lifting directly into your own stateful code. Staleness-based eviction: since an aircraft leaving a zone generates no leave event, a recurring sweep evicts anything not seen within a short TTL. And idempotent timers: since handleInputRows fires once per row, only registering a timer if one isn't already pending keeps exactly one sweep alive instead of piling up thousands.
